explanations.explanation: This neuron fires whenever the model sees a “weird” subword piece—i.e. a non-ASCII or foreign-script character (diacritic, combining mark, Cyrillic, Arabic, Thai, Japanese kana/kanji, etc.). It acts as a generic flag for out-of-ordinary Unicode fragments.

This neuron detects the boilerplate “placeholder page” pattern—i.e. template copy signaling a stub or missing profile page (“This is a placeholder page for …”) and related notices about automatically generated, empty content.

This feature fires on the little “dot” when it’s used inside tokens—e.g. in abbreviations (U.S., Nov.), initials (W.E.), decimals/measurements (16.9, 31.8%, 3.0, 3.6 L) or version numbers—i.e. a period that’s part of a composite token rather than ending a sentence.

This neuron fires whenever the model sees a consonant‐heavy subword (often a pure or near-pure consonant cluster) – the little “chunks” you get in BPE tokenization of names, technical terms or agglutinative suffixes (asp in “Kaspersky,” har in “Bharavi,” ipl in “whiplash,” the w in “Botswana,” the t in Turkish –tır–, etc.). It’s basically a detector for those dense-consonant subword pieces.

This feature is essentially a little “consonant‐cluster” detector at the character level.  It lights up on multi‐letter sequences like ph-, qu-, scr-, ch-, ur-, gu-, alac-, auc-, etc. – the kinds of uncommon consonant clusters that tend to occur at the starts (or inside) of Greek/Latin‐derived English words and proper names.

This neuron lights up on the very first subtoken of a capitalized or all-caps term—i.e. the initial letter(s) of titles, headers, acronyms, brand or product names, recipe‐step labels, etc.—serving as a “start-of-named-entity/section” marker.
This feature detects the sentence-final full stop—the “.” token that marks the end of a declarative sentence or standalone heading/title.

This neuron responds to typographic name‐markers—tokens like all‐caps acronyms, initialisms, trademarked or branded terms, and standardized proper nouns (e.g. “IoT,” “Core™ i7,” “U.S.,” “Access™/Excel™,” “Western blot,” “SEC,” “Ph.D.”). It flags tokens that signal technical standards, corporate/product names, legal or organizational abbreviations, and other uppercase or trademarked entities.

This feature fires on the stems or suffixes of technical nouns—especially the second halves of compound scientific or specialized terms (e.g. “-mitter” in neurotransmitter, “-amin” in vitamin, “-usion” in diffusion, “-ptin” in leptin, “-antibody,” etc.)—serving as a detector for key domain-specific vocabulary.
This feature is a detector for informal verb contractions—especially negations (don’t, doesn’t, isn’t)—that signal a conversational tone.

This feature is basically a sub-token “AR” detector.  It lights up whenever the letters “ar” (or closely related fragments like “der,” “Far,” “al,” etc.) appear as a standalone token or subword—very common in names (van der Merwe, McFarland, Margarita, Mont(al)ban, van der Waals, etc.)—and even on the slash “/” when it’s being used as a tight separator (as in “indoor/outdoor” or “A/C”).
This feature detects sentence-final full stops (the period “.” that marks the end of a sentence).
This neuron simply detects the full-stop “.” token—i.e. period punctuation marking sentence (or title/heading) boundaries and abbreviation separators.

This feature fires on the main “defining” verbs (copulas and simple-past predicates like is/was/were, registered, voted, worked, served, etc.) that introduce factual descriptions or definitions of an entity—i.e. the head predicate in the lead sentence of an encyclopedic or news‐style statement.

This neuron fires on the very first token of a structured heading or list entry—titles, bullet points or category labels—across languages (Korean, English, Russian, etc.), signaling the start of an itemized/heading block.

This neuron is a subword‐fragment detector that lights up on the little two‐ or three‐letter BPE pieces you see inside longer proper names (e.g. “ne” in Disney, “or” in Conor, “und” in Arundel, “ig” in Antigua, “ug” in Murugan, “les” in Middlesbrough, etc.). It’s effectively signalling those mid‐word/name subtoken patterns that crop up in many named entities.

This neuron lights up on core action‐verbs that signal formal decisions or status changes by an agent or organization (e.g. discontinue, suspend, approve, recover, appreciate, decline, gain, slow, drop, give).

This neuron is essentially a CJK‐script detector – it lights up on Chinese characters (Han/Kanji), Japanese kana/kanji and Korean Hangul tokens (e.g. category headers, forum/UI labels, mixed English–Chinese name displays, etc.).

This feature lights up on verbs and phrases where the writer voices a personal takeaway or judgment—e.g. “I learned,” “I love,” “I really enjoyed,” “have you heard,” “would recommend”—marking moments of subjective evaluation, discovery or endorsement.
This neuron detects sentence-initial imperative verbs—especially “See,” “Put,” and “Let”—marking calls-to-action or instructional openings.
